newsitem.title: ESTONIA: Estonia hails EU decision as "new impulse".
newsitem.headline: Estonia hails EU decision as "new impulse".

text.p: The tiny former Soviet Baltic state of Estonia hailed on Wednesday a decision to ask it to European Union entry talks as a new impulse to the reforms which have earned it the name the "Baltic Tiger".
"It gives us a new impulse and at the same time a duty and responsibility successfully to complete the negotiations if they start," Prime Minister Mart Siimann told a news conference.
Estonia, which quit the former Soviet Union in 1991, was the only ex-Soviet state asked to talks with four former Communist bloc nations: Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovenia.
The country of just 1.5 million has been seen as the regional leader for some time but an International Monetary Fund (IMF) official warned against complacency.
Estonia's push for independence, along with that of fellow Baltic states Latvia and Lithuania, heralded the beginning of the end for the Soviet empire.
But it later stole a march on its neighbours by launching radical free market reforms, pushing most ahead with privatisation and the creation of an open, market economy.
The foreign ministry said it "greatly appreciated" the Commission's decision.

"Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Toomas Hendrik Ilves has stressed that Estonia must continue at the same speed and has still a long way to go in its integration with European structures," the ministry added.
The move to integrate Estonia into the EU was seen as a vote of confidence in its reforms but International Monetary Fund (IMF) representative Dimitri Demekas warned against complacency.
"A lot needs to be done," he said, noting that the country had a large and rising trade and current account deficit, which the Commission also highlighted in its report on the country.
"This (the Commission decision) won't make much difference on a day-to-day level, they are already on the right track," he said, adding there was no reason to relax.

Siimann said the Commission's recommendation was also positive for Latvia and Lithuania, left out of the first wave of countries to be invited to EU entry talks but also seen as reform-minded, Western-oriented nations.
"It would not have a bad impact on Latvia and Lithuania as Estonia can later give them support in their aspirations for EU membership," he said.
